subtitle: Culture includes the meanings and expectations people learn, including those built into the way work gets done. This introduction helps you begin noticing them in everyday situations, including your own workplace habits.
scope: For staff across DHS. Use practice or appropriately shareable examples to examine work routines; do not disclose private client, employee or medical information. These activities support learning and do not assess an individual’s IDI orientation or create a personnel score. Formal policy, accommodation and workplace concerns retain their responsible procedures. Matters involving Native American communities or Tribal relations should be referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: Culture includes more than food, festivals or nationality. It also appears in learned meanings, familiar ways of relating and expectations people may take for granted. Staff and the organizations they work in have cultural patterns too. This course helps you recognize those patterns without assuming that every member of a group thinks alike. You will examine a workplace routine, check an interpretation, consider more than one explanation and choose a bounded next step. The purpose is not to become an expert on other people’s identities. It is to make your own work more thoughtful and usable while keeping decisions, evidence and responsibility clear.

intro.heading: Recognize culture beyond what is easy to see
intro.body:
Culture is often introduced through visible features: a language, a meal, a celebration or a style of dress. Those features can be meaningful, but they are only part of the subject. Culture also concerns how people learn to interpret a situation, relate to others and understand what is expected. UNESCO’s broad definition includes ways of living together and systems of meaning. It does not reduce culture to a list of national customs.

Consider a practice workgroup that expects every participant to challenge a draft aloud as soon as it is shown. Longtime members regard this as useful collaboration. A new member thinks a written review after reading the draft is the more responsible contribution. The difference might involve learned expectations about preparation and disagreement. It might also involve access to the material or the amount of time available. Neither explanation can be established by looking at the person.

Start by describing the routine and the expectation. What does the group treat as a helpful response? How do people learn that expectation? Which other ways of contributing could meet the work’s purpose? You are examining an arrangement, not diagnosing a colleague. A pattern becomes useful when it helps you form a better question and examine the actual evidence.

Do not turn the idea of shared culture into a claim that members are identical. People disagree, draw on different experiences and change practices. A cultural reference can help someone describe their own experience; it cannot authorize you to invent that account for them. In DHS work, the immediate learning task is often small: notice one expectation you assumed was obvious and make its purpose understandable.

flashcards.back: Learned and shared meanings, practices and expectations associated with groups and everyday life; members can interpret and change them differently.
A recurring way of making meaning or acting that can guide a question without predicting every person.
The affiliations and aspects of experience a person may use to understand themselves; another person should not assign their meaning automatically.
What you can describe from the situation before explaining its cause or meaning.
An explanation you give an observation, which may need to be checked.
An expected way of doing work that may feel obvious to people already familiar with it.

items.title: A visible practice
items.body: A meeting opens with introductions. That is observable, but its meaning is not fixed. One participant may value connection; another may need to know each person’s role in the decision. Ask what the introduction is intended to accomplish before concluding that attendance or enthusiasm proves a shared value.

items.title: An expectation that feels neutral
items.body: A team considers an immediate spoken response the normal sign of preparation. That norm may be familiar rather than essential. For a practice draft review, compare it with a timely written response that identifies the same evidence. The comparison tests the work need without ranking personalities.

items.title: A shared pattern with variation
items.body: Several colleagues describe learning to avoid public disagreement. Their accounts can suggest a useful question about review channels. They do not establish what every colleague from the same background prefers. Keep each account scoped and examine how the current work arrangement allows a meaningful response.

tabs.label: Visible feature
tabs.body: Describe what is present, such as the language used in a notice or the format of a meeting. Visibility gives you something to examine, but it does not establish motive or meaning. A bilingual heading, for example, does not by itself show that the entire process is usable.

tabs.label: Meaning
tabs.body: Ask what the feature or routine means to participants in this situation. Different people may interpret the same introduction as welcome, required performance or a way to understand authority. A meaning question improves understanding; it should not require anyone to explain their identity.

tabs.label: Work consequence
tabs.body: Connect the pattern to a practical effect that can be examined. If useful comments arrive after a meeting, the team can examine the review window and materials. It need not decide which culture caused the timing. The result can be a clearer opportunity to contribute.

check.question: A colleague gives written feedback instead of speaking during a draft meeting. What can you conclude?
check.correct: The format is observable; its meaning and suitability need to be examined in relation to the situation and work.
wrong: Written feedback always indicates greater competence.
check.feedbackCorrect: This separates what happened from the meaning you supplied and keeps the inquiry connected to the work.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Nationality does not establish an individual’s reason. Calling the response poor teamwork converts an unfamiliar format into a personal judgment. Treating written work as always superior makes the opposite shortcut. Examine the content, timing and agreed work purpose before deciding what the format enabled or missed.

items.text: The feedback arrived in a written note.
The participant may have wanted time to examine the evidence.
Everyone from that community avoids teamwork.
The meeting invited immediate verbal comments.
The team may associate speaking quickly with preparation.
One person’s response proves the whole group’s values.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Leah receives a useful written review from Tomas after a draft meeting. She initially calls him disengaged because he did not speak in the meeting. The comments identify a missing source that affects the recommendation.
options: Whether the feedback met the work purpose, how the review opportunity was explained and what Leah assumed about participation.
Whether silence should automatically reduce a future performance rating.
responses: A presumed group trait does not explain this person’s response or the quality of the review.
This examines the actual contribution and the expectation without making a personal cultural conclusion.
A learning discussion does not authorize a personnel judgment, and silence alone is not the required work evidence.

lessons.transfer: Use a practice routine to name one visible feature, one possible meaning and one question that could check the meaning.

move.control: You can describe a routine and question your interpretation before assigning a meaning to another person.
move.failure: Culture becomes a catalogue of traits used to judge individuals.
move.next: Notice one work expectation you regard as obvious and explain its practical purpose.

intro.heading: Find learned expectations in everyday work
intro.body:
A work routine can become so familiar that staff stop noticing how a newcomer learns it. The team may know which questions belong in a meeting, who receives a draft first and when a concern is considered timely. These expectations can be learned through repeated interactions rather than a written instruction. Calling them normal does not explain their purpose to someone who has not shared that history.

In a practice policy workgroup, a draft invitation says “send comments through the usual route.” Longtime members know which mailbox is checked and which colleague can clarify a question. A new employee uses a different mailbox and receives no response. The problem is not evidence that the employee lacks judgment. The invitation relied on information that was never made available.

Examine the expectation in three parts: the required result, the route and the reason. A formal approval requirement may be necessary because a designated role has authority. A preference for a particular discussion style may be open to another method that achieves the same result. Confirm actual policy and responsible guidance before proposing a change; the course does not authorize staff to waive requirements or alter access rules.

Make a useful expectation visible. For the practice invitation, name the mailbox, the type of response needed, the responsible contact and how a person will know the contribution was received. Ask a colleague to explain the next step in their own words without treating that as a competence test. If the explanation exposes an instruction gap, revise the instruction. The aim is a dependable route, not a demand that everyone already know the team’s habits.

lessons.keyStatement: Explain what the work requires instead of relying on people to learn a hidden rule.

items.title: The phrase everyone understands
items.body: “Use the usual process” works only for people who know what usual means. In a practice briefing review, a newcomer may need the actual contact and the decision question. Replace the inherited phrase with the route and purpose rather than blaming the employee for not sharing the team’s history.

items.title: A necessary formal step
items.body: A designated role may need to approve a policy decision. That requirement should remain in its responsible process. You can still explain what the person responsible needs and where questions go. Making a rule understandable is different from granting yourself authority to remove it.

items.title: A preferred style
items.body: A team may prefer comments delivered orally, although the task needs an accurate account of evidence. Compare whether an agreed written route meets that need. Keep the standard of useful analysis while examining whether the familiar format is essential or simply inherited.

tabs.label: Keep the purpose
tabs.body: Begin with the result the routine serves: an accurate briefing, a recorded decision or timely coordination. Without that purpose, a change may improve comfort but miss a real dependency. A newcomer’s question can help make the purpose explicit without eliminating the responsibility.

tabs.label: Explain the route
tabs.body: State the contact, material and next step so insider knowledge is less necessary. For example, a practice review invitation can name where questions go and what response the sender can expect. This improves usability while preserving the appropriate approval and information-handling routes.

tabs.label: Examine the preference
tabs.body: Check whether the familiar method is the only way to achieve the purpose. An alternative may be usable, or it may create a new dependency. Compare the actual tradeoff and seek responsible guidance when a formal requirement is involved; do not assume every preference can be removed instantly.

check.question: A draft invitation says “use the usual route,” and new staff cannot find it. What is the useful next step?
check.correct: Explain the actual route and work purpose, check whether the instruction is usable and preserve any formal requirements.
wrong: Tell new staff to absorb the culture without asking questions.
Remove every approval requirement because it feels unfamiliar.
Choose a route based on presumed cultural identity.
check.feedbackCorrect: This addresses the instruction gap while retaining the legitimate work result and authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Absorbing the culture is not an explanation of an unavailable route. Removing every requirement confuses a communication gap with authority to change policy. An identity-based route guesses needs instead of making a usable instruction available. Clarify the shared purpose and actual process first.

items.text: Send it where we always send it.
Send the evidence summary to the named review contact and ask there about missing information.
Confirm who may approve a proposed policy change.
You should already know when concerns are welcome.
The invitation explains the open decision and response route.
Check whether a requested format is a formal requirement.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Nina is new to a practice DHS workgroup. The invitation names no contact and says to follow the usual review path. Her questions are described as a lack of fit, although no one can show her the route.
options: Make the review path and purpose understandable, invite a process question and keep formal approval responsibilities intact.
Tell Nina that asking shows she does not belong.
Let Nina approve the policy herself to remove the confusion.
responses: This fixes the information arrangement instead of inventing a trait or bypassing authority.
Belonging is not established by guessing an unwritten route.
The confusion does not create approval authority; a clearer route is the relevant repair.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite a practice “usual process” instruction with its purpose, route, contact and formal boundary.

move.control: You can make an instruction understandable and seek guidance about its real requirements.
move.failure: Insider knowledge is treated as a measure of who belongs.
move.next: Choose one routine instruction and check whether a newcomer can find the next step.

Identify a demand that makes one person represent a whole community.

Check meaning without demanding personal disclosure.
One person’s account has a scope.
lessons.statement: Use a cultural idea to improve your question, not to finish someone else’s story.

intro.heading: Use patterns as questions rather than personal scripts
intro.body:
Learning about cultural patterns can help staff notice assumptions. It becomes misleading when a general description is used as a script for an individual. A person may recognize a pattern, disagree with it or find it irrelevant to the present situation. Their experience also includes professional roles, relationships and circumstances that a broad category cannot describe.

Imagine a colleague who asks for a written account of a decision. Another staff member has read that some communities value indirect communication and decides the request must reflect that pattern. The observation is only that a written account was requested. The colleague might need an accurate record, time to review evidence or a clearer explanation of authority. A cultural possibility should remain a possibility until appropriate evidence supports it.

Ask about the situation in neutral terms: what would make the decision account useful, or which part of the current explanation needs clarification? Do not ask why people from the colleague’s background behave that way. That wording makes a group claim and gives the person responsibility for explaining it. Allow the colleague to answer without an identity story.

If someone voluntarily explains a cultural connection, listen and preserve its scope. You can say that this account helped you understand this interaction. You cannot turn it into a universal rule for all staff with a similar identity. Use established resources and relevant expertise for broader inquiry, and do not put speculative cultural labels in personnel or client records. A better question can improve the work without requiring an assessment of the person.

lessons.keyStatement: Use a cultural idea to improve your question, not to finish someone else’s story.

items.title: A useful general idea
items.body: A resource suggests that expectations about disagreement can vary. Use that idea to examine how a practice meeting invites challenge. Ask which channels allow participants to raise a concern. The resource does not tell you which employee wants which channel or whether a particular silence has cultural meaning.

items.title: A personal script
items.body: A supervisor decides that a quiet employee will not want a visible assignment because of an assumed community norm. The shortcut can remove an opportunity without hearing the person. Explain the assignment and its requirements through the appropriate route; do not substitute a group description for their actual interest.

items.title: A voluntary account
items.body: A colleague chooses to share an experience of learning to avoid public contradiction. That can inform this discussion, but the person has not agreed to educate everyone about a community. Thank them for the scoped insight and use other learning resources for broader questions.

tabs.label: Assume
tabs.body: An assumed explanation can feel efficient because it removes uncertainty. It also creates a risk of responding to a person you imagined. If a colleague asks for a written decision, treating the request as a cultural trait may overlook a missing work record or unclear responsibility.

tabs.label: Ask
tabs.body: A neutral question keeps more than one explanation open. Ask what information is needed for the task and how it will be used. This can reveal a practical requirement without requiring a personal identity account. The person remains free to share only what is relevant.

tabs.label: Respond
tabs.body: Choose a response supported by the information available. If the task needs a clear decision record, provide it through the appropriate process rather than designing an identity-based exception. If meaning remains uncertain, state the limit and check the work result instead of claiming cultural expertise.

check.question: A colleague asks for a written decision account. What question best checks the meaning?
check.correct: Which information would make the decision account useful for your next work step?
wrong: Why does everyone from your background avoid direct communication?
Which IDI stage explains this request?
Should I assume that you never want to speak in meetings?
check.feedbackCorrect: The question focuses on the actual task and leaves room for the colleague’s meaning without a group script.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The group question assigns a representative burden and assumes the cause. An IDI stage cannot be inferred from a request or administered by this activity. Assuming a permanent preference turns one interaction into a personal rule. Ask about the present work need and keep any account appropriately scoped.

items.text: Which part of the decision needs clarification?
People with that background never want visible assignments.
Explain what everyone in your community thinks.
What would help you complete the next task?
A written request always means indirectness.
You must teach the whole team about your identity.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Sam asks for a clearer record of a practice project decision. Jo assumes that Sam’s background explains the request and asks him to describe his whole community’s communication rules. The team has not recorded which option was selected.
options: Keep the community question because it sounds interested.
Ask what work information is missing and create the appropriate decision record without demanding an identity explanation.
responses: Interest does not remove the unsupported group premise or representative burden.
A work request is not an individual assessment, and the course does not infer orientations.
This addresses the practical gap and respects Sam’s choice about any personal account.

lessons.transfer: Describe a practice observation, two possible explanations and a neutral question. Write the limit on what one answer could establish.

move.control: You can check an interpretation and use resources without making a colleague represent a group.
move.failure: A cultural reference replaces evidence about the actual person and task.
move.next: Before responding to an unfamiliar approach, name what you observed separately from your explanation.

lessons.title: Consider multiple affiliations and changing situations
lessons.summary: Describe how one person may draw on more than one affiliation.
lessons.objective: Describe how one person may draw on more than one affiliation.
objectives: Describe how one person may draw on more than one affiliation.
Identify a situational explanation for a changed work response.
Avoid treating context-dependent behavior as a fixed cultural trait.
takeaways: People belong to more than one group.
The relevance of an affiliation can change by situation.
A change in response needs context before explanation.
lessons.statement: A person’s participation in culture is more complex than a single category.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Consider multiple affiliations and changing situations
intro.body:
A person may participate in a family, profession, workplace, language community and several other groups. These affiliations can overlap without having the same meaning in every situation. Council of Europe educational material emphasizes that cultures have internal variation and that people’s affiliations are context-dependent. A single category therefore cannot provide a complete account of an individual’s experience.

In a practice DHS discussion, a financial analyst speaks cautiously about an uncertain cost estimate but gives a clear recommendation about a completed reconciliation. A colleague interprets the cautious response as a permanent cultural reluctance to decide. The actual difference may be the quality of evidence and the analyst’s professional responsibility. The person can be cautious in one situation and decisive in another without contradiction.

Look at what changed. Was the question the same? Did the evidence, audience, authority or responsibility differ? Consider these explanations before asking for personal background. Multiple affiliations are not a requirement to collect an identity inventory. The work question may be answered by understanding the task and the information available.

When a person chooses to describe an affiliation, let them explain its meaning and relevance. Do not decide which identity should matter most or insist that their response proves membership in a group. A respectful inquiry can acknowledge cultural meaning and still leave room for variation. The practical result is a more accurate interpretation and a response that fits the present work.

Identify a situational explanation for a changed work response.
Avoid treating context-dependent behavior as a fixed cultural trait.
Which response is most useful?
lessons.keyStatement: A person’s participation in culture is more complex than a single category.

items.title: The role changes the response
items.body: An employee may ask more questions when accountable for a financial figure than when joining an informal learning discussion. Compare the responsibility and evidence before interpreting the difference. The practice case illustrates a situational question; it does not claim that every analyst behaves alike.

items.title: An affiliation has different relevance
items.body: A language community may matter to one conversation while a professional role matters to another. The person can explain that relevance if they choose. Asking for a complete identity profile adds information the task may not need and can make learning feel like compulsory disclosure.

items.title: A group contains disagreement
items.body: Colleagues in the same unit may hold different views about how to review a draft. Membership does not eliminate personal experience or differences in role. Examine the options and effects instead of calling disagreement proof that one person is less authentic or less committed to the group.

tabs.label: Single label
tabs.body: A single label may make a complex interaction seem easy to explain. It can also hide differences in responsibility and available evidence. In the practice estimate case, calling caution a permanent group trait bypasses the actual uncertainty that a responsible analysis should name.

tabs.label: Context
tabs.body: Check the task, audience, evidence and authority. This may reveal why the same person responds differently without collecting private information. Context is not a guarantee that culture is irrelevant; it prevents culture from becoming the only explanation before the situation is understood.

tabs.label: Person’s account
tabs.body: A person’s own account can add meaning, and the person decides what to share. Keep the explanation connected to this situation and do not translate it into a fixed employee category. Their account and the work evidence can inform a response without a cultural profile.

check.question: A colleague is cautious with an uncertain estimate and decisive with a verified figure. What should you examine?
check.correct: The evidence and responsibility in each situation before explaining the difference as a fixed cultural trait.
wrong: Whether their identity changed between meetings.
Whether cautious people should always be excluded from decisions.
Which single community label explains every response.
check.feedbackCorrect: This considers the relevant context and avoids turning varied participation into an unsupported permanent trait.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Identity does not need to change for a response to change. Exclusion converts one cautious response into an opportunity rule without evidence. A single community label cannot establish every work meaning. Compare the task and evidence, and ask a relevant question if something remains unclear.

items.text: The estimate has several unresolved inputs.
This person never makes decisions because of their background.
Provide a complete cultural identity profile before we hear the estimate.
The employee has formal responsibility for the accuracy of the figure.
All members of the unit must think the same way.
Prove which identity matters most to you.

lessons.next: Next: Keep culture, access and responsibility distinct

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Avery asks careful questions about a practice cost estimate but makes a clear choice when the data are verified. Pat describes Avery as culturally indecisive and wants an identity questionnaire. The estimate contains unresolved inputs.
options: Compare the evidence, responsibility and question in each situation, then clarify the uncertain inputs without assigning a trait.
Keep the label because it simplifies the discussion.
Require a personal profile before examining the estimate.
responses: This makes the actual difference examinable and keeps private identity disclosure out of an unnecessary work inquiry.
A simpler label can be inaccurate and obscure a real evidence gap.
The work uncertainty does not require a complete identity account.

lessons.transfer: Compare two practice situations involving the same person. Name the changed task, evidence or responsibility and what you cannot conclude about identity.

move.control: You can examine context and invite a relevant account without reducing a person to one affiliation.
move.failure: Variation becomes a reason to question authenticity or assign a fixed trait.
move.next: Check what changed in the situation before explaining a changed response.

lessons.title: Keep culture, access and responsibility distinct

Choose an appropriate learning or formal-process response to a practice concern.
takeaways: More than one explanation may be relevant.
Respecting culture does not excuse harmful conduct.
Access and formal concerns need their responsible routes.
lessons.statement: Understanding meaning supports responsible action; it does not replace evidence or duties.

intro.heading: Keep culture, access and responsibility distinct
intro.body:
Culture can help staff examine meaning, but it should not become the explanation for every difficulty. A person may be unable to use a meeting format because of an inaccessible document, a missing language service, a schedule conflict or unavailable information. Treating that difficulty as a cultural preference can leave the actual barrier unchanged. Different explanations require different questions and, sometimes, different responsible processes.

Consider a practice training invitation with a document that cannot be used by one participant. The facilitator guesses that the person prefers not to participate because of a cultural value. The useful first question is whether the material and participation route are usable. Do not require the person to explain a diagnosis or identity before following the applicable access or accommodation process. Formal requests and information must be handled through current procedures.

Respect for cultural difference also has boundaries. It does not excuse threats, discrimination or harassment, and an unfamiliar communication style does not automatically prove those harms. Examine what occurred and follow the responsibilities that apply. Managers and supervisors must immediately report alleged discrimination or harassment covered by MMB’s policy to agency HR or the affirmative action officer. A learning conversation should not become an informal investigation or a required step before reporting.

Match the response to the issue. A meaning question can help with an uncertain interpretation. A clearer instruction can address missing work information. An access request or formal concern needs its responsible route, and practical respectful support can continue alongside it. The consultant can provide guidance while staff retain their work and managers retain their duties. Knowing which question you are asking helps avoid both cultural overclaiming and a failure to act.

lessons.keyStatement: Understanding meaning supports responsible action; it does not replace evidence or duties.

items.title: A practical barrier
items.body: A document is not usable in the participant’s format. Guessing a cultural preference does not fix it. Use the applicable accessibility or accommodation route and handle personal information appropriately. A practice can examine the design without using real medical details or making a formal determination.

items.title: An uncertain interpretation
items.body: A direct question feels unfamiliar but its words and effect are not yet clear. Ask about the task and intended meaning while maintaining respectful conduct expectations. Do not infer misconduct solely from unfamiliar style, and do not decide that every conflict must be cultural.

items.title: An alleged prohibited act
items.body: If a manager receives an allegation of discrimination or harassment within MMB Policy 1436, immediate reporting to agency HR or the affirmative action officer is required. Do not promise secrecy or ask the person to finish this course before reporting. Learning can support respectful behavior without replacing the designated response.

tabs.label: Learn about meaning
tabs.body: Use a neutral question when an interpretation is uncertain. This route may clarify why someone chose a format or how a message was understood. It is insufficient if the problem is an unusable document or an allegation that carries formal responsibilities. Curiosity should not postpone the appropriate response.

tabs.label: Improve access
tabs.body: Examine the material and route people need to use. A format barrier can require a responsible access or accommodation process rather than an identity explanation. Preserve confidentiality and current requirements; do not claim that a universal learning design automatically resolves every individual request.

tabs.label: Follow responsibility
tabs.body: Formal concerns have designated routes and duties. A cultural explanation does not authorize a manager to keep an allegation informal. Immediate reporting and an appropriate practical response can proceed alongside learning, without labeling either person or making a course an access gate.

check.question: A manager receives an allegation of discrimination during a learning discussion. What should happen?
check.correct: Immediately report it to agency HR or the affirmative action officer under the applicable policy and keep learning separate from the formal response.
wrong: Resolve it by deciding which cultural orientation caused it.
Promise secrecy so the discussion feels safe.
Require the employee to finish the course before reporting.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response preserves the actual reporting duty without using a learning activity to make a formal finding.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An inferred orientation neither explains nor investigates an allegation. Secrecy can conflict with the manager’s immediate reporting responsibility. Requiring course completion creates an improper gate to the formal route. Respond respectfully, report through the designated process and avoid unnecessary disclosure.

items.text: Ask which part of a work instruction was unclear.
Follow the appropriate route for an unusable document format.
A manager immediately reports an alleged covered discriminatory act to agency HR or the affirmative action officer.
Check what a colleague meant by a particular work phrase.
Confirm a usable participation option through applicable procedures.
Keep actual personnel information within its approved handling rules.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: During a practice course discussion, Elena tells supervisor Marcus that she experienced discrimination. Marcus wants to interpret the issue as a difference in communication and asks Elena to complete a reflection before he takes it further.
options: Keep it inside the reflection activity.
Immediately report the allegation through the designated HR or affirmative action route and offer appropriate practical support without conducting an informal investigation.
Assign both people an IDI orientation to explain the concern.
responses: The course cannot become a condition for the formal response or replace the reporting duty.
This preserves Marcus’s duty and distinguishes support from a formal determination.
A learning tool cannot infer orientations or establish the cause of alleged discrimination.

lessons.transfer: For three practice concerns, name whether the next step is a meaning question, access response or formal route. Explain any overlap without using personal details.

move.control: You can ask an appropriate question and follow duties without turning culture into an all-purpose explanation.
move.failure: A cultural discussion hides an access barrier or delays a formal responsibility.
move.next: When a concern arises, distinguish what needs understanding from what needs an immediate responsible response.

intro.heading: Complete a bounded culture-and-assumption inquiry
intro.body:
The earlier lessons offer a way to examine culture without profiling people. Begin with one routine you touch: a review invitation, a meeting instruction or a response channel. Describe what happens and the expectation built into it. Then name an assumption that could affect use of the routine. Keep the inquiry narrow enough to examine through appropriate evidence and an action within your role.

For a practice draft review, the observation might be that material is first shown during the meeting. The assumption is that participants can understand and respond immediately. The evidence question is whether contributors have a usable chance to examine the draft and raise relevant concerns. Do not explain the pattern by assigning identities or counting guessed cultural groups. A clear process question can be examined without that information.

Compare an appropriate option with the current arrangement. Sharing an approved draft earlier may improve review time, but it also requires an owner, an appropriate version and permitted access. Offering a written response route may help but still needs a decision question and a response owner. Choose the change for its relation to the work, not because you believe a presumed group always prefers it. Confirm formal requirements before acting.

Check the result and preserve uncertainty. Did the next review receive useful questions before the choice closed? Did the response owner explain what happened to them? Those findings can support a process improvement. They do not prove that every person feels included, that bias is gone or that someone reached an IDI orientation. Staff perform their own inquiry; consultant feedback is available without becoming a universal review gate. The lasting practice is to observe, question, examine and follow through.

inThisLesson: Write a work inquiry with observation, assumption and evidence need.
Choose a proportionate next action within actual authority.

What should the report say?
lessons.keyStatement: A practical inquiry improves an arrangement while remaining honest about what it cannot establish.

items.title: A small inquiry with substance
items.body: The practice review question focuses on when people can examine a draft and how their concerns reach the owner. It is small, but it can affect the evidence available to a decision. A narrower inquiry can produce a more credible improvement than a broad claim about the entire team’s cultural competence.

items.title: An action within responsibility
items.body: An employee can clarify an invitation within their task and seek approval for an earlier shareable draft. They cannot change information permissions or waive formal review on their own. The inquiry should identify the decision owner and any necessary guidance before the proposed option becomes an action.

items.title: A qualified result
items.body: Useful feedback before the decision is one result to examine. Missing responses remain unknown, and additional timing or workload factors may matter. Describe the observed effect and its limits rather than declaring a universal cultural transformation. This leaves a clearer foundation for the next inquiry.

tabs.label: Current arrangement
tabs.body: Describe the existing route and its purpose before changing it. A meeting-only review may support coordination while leaving little time to examine a complex draft. Understanding both effects keeps the comparison fair and avoids assuming that the familiar process has no value.

tabs.label: Proposed option
tabs.body: Explain how the option addresses the assumption and what it requires. Earlier access to an approved draft can create useful review time but needs an owner and appropriate permissions. A new route should be usable, lawful and connected to the decision rather than added as a symbolic gesture.

tabs.label: Result and limit
tabs.body: Choose a check tied to the work, such as whether relevant questions were examined before the decision. Record missing evidence and alternative influences honestly. A favorable result supports a bounded improvement, not a personal developmental label or a claim that every barrier has disappeared.

check.question: A team receives more useful questions after sharing a practice review draft earlier. What is the supported conclusion?
check.correct: Earlier draft access may have improved this review opportunity; examine the response and other relevant conditions before making a broader claim.
wrong: Every team member has reached Adaptation.
All cultural barriers are permanently eliminated.
Missing responses prove that everyone else is satisfied.
check.feedbackCorrect: This keeps the result connected to the observed arrangement and acknowledges what the evidence does not establish.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A process result cannot place individuals on the IDC. One improved review does not establish permanent elimination of every barrier. Missing responses provide no reassurance about satisfaction. Preserve the actual finding and examine follow-through, limits and the next relevant question.

items.text: Check whether the draft was available before the review decision.
One meeting proves every employee has the same cultural needs.
Confirm permitted draft access and assign a response owner.
Ask which instruction was unclear without requiring an identity story.
No response means no concern.
Review whether useful questions received an explained answer.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to examine a routine with clear questions, appropriate evidence and follow-through.

scenario.context: Consider this situation: A DHS team shares an approved draft before a review meeting and receives a useful question about missing evidence. Director Ren wants to report that all staff have reached an advanced intercultural stage. Several participants did not respond, and the effect of timing has not been separated from other changes.
options: The team has reached a single cultural stage.
Describe the changed review arrangement and useful question, explain limits and check whether the issue received a responsible response.
responses: The activity does not assess individual or group IDI orientations.
Nonresponse has several possible explanations and cannot establish an attitude.
This makes the real improvement visible while preserving uncertainty and follow-through.

lessons.transfer: Complete a practice inquiry with routine, observation, assumption, evidence question, option, authority, owner and result check. Add one sentence about what the inquiry cannot establish.

move.control: You can conduct a bounded work inquiry and request guidance while retaining responsibility for the task.
move.failure: A useful practice becomes an unsupported score or a universal success claim.
move.next: Choose one routine, examine one assumption and make one evidence-linked improvement within your role.

jobAid.subtitle: Examine culture in a work routine without profiling the people involved.
remember: Culture includes meaning and expectations, not only visible customs.
A group pattern does not tell you an individual’s meaning.
Learning does not replace formal responsibilities or assess IDI orientations.

sections.heading: Observe and ask
items: Name one routine and its work purpose.
Describe what happened before explaining it.
Identify the learned expectation you may be taking for granted.
Ask a neutral question that does not require personal disclosure.

sections.heading: Examine the situation
items: Consider task, information, access, role and authority as well as possible cultural meaning.
Keep a voluntary account scoped to the person and situation.
Distinguish a preference from a formal requirement.
Follow access, accommodation and reporting duties through their responsible routes.

sections.heading: Act and review
items: Choose an option tied to the actual evidence and within your authority.
Name the owner and necessary guidance.
Check the practical work result and explain missing evidence.
Do not create a personal cultural profile or a claim that every barrier has disappeared.

sources.title: UNESCO — Universal Declaration on Cultural Diversity
sources.note: Broad international conceptual reference for culture and the human-rights boundary. It does not establish Minnesota operational procedures.

sources.title: Council of Europe — Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Explores multiple affiliations, variation within cultures and context, especially pages 13–17. The DHS examples apply these ideas for learning; they are not copied exercises or agency mandates.

sources.title: IDI — Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: Official five-orientation learning reference. These course activities do not administer or infer an individual IDI assessment. Integration, where discussed elsewhere in this program, means the people a process affects help design it; it is not an additional official IDC orientation.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Statewide policy states managers’ and supervisors’ immediate reporting duty for covered allegations to agency HR or the affirmative action officer. Learning activity does not replace the designated process.

sources.title: Minnesota DHS — Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency requirements continue to apply. Required equity review, training and responsible decision-making still apply.
